You manage a 12-person marketing team adopting an AI assistant. Last year the team's vendor updated its models three times, and each update made parts of the team's shared "best prompts" document obsolete. You are planning this year's AI training investment.

Which approach best reflects the course's rationale for AI Fluency?

A. Rebuild the prompt template library after each model update and require the team to use only approved templates.
B. Postpone training until model capabilities stabilize, so the material stays accurate longer.
C. Limit AI use to two power users who keep up with each model's quirks and handle requests for everyone else.
D. Develop the team's durable competencies in deciding what to delegate, communicating intent, evaluating outputs, and acting responsibly.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D matches the course's core premise: AI Fluency is a lasting framework of competencies (the 4Ds of Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence) that stays relevant as AI technology evolves, unlike temporary tips and tricks. Option A doubles down on exactly the tips-and-tricks knowledge the scenario shows going stale with every model update. Option B misreads the landscape, since capabilities keep evolving and the framework is designed for that condition. Option C concentrates fragile model-specific knowledge in two people instead of building transferable skills across the team.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration)

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. You configure an AI assistant with your organization's background, voice guidelines, and standard response procedures so it can handle routine donor inquiries on the team's behalf, rather than giving it one task at a time.

Which way of engaging with AI does this arrangement represent?

A. Automation
B. Augmentation
C. Agency
D. Delegation
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Agency means configuring AI to work independently on your behalf, establishing its knowledge and behavior patterns rather than issuing specific task instructions, which is exactly what this setup describes. Option A, Automation, is the AI completing specific tasks based on your direct instructions, the pattern this arrangement moves beyond. Option B, Augmentation, is back-and-forth collaboration in which you and the AI work as thinking and task-execution partners. Option D, Delegation, is not one of the three ways of engaging at all; it is one of the 4D competencies, the skill of deciding what work to do with AI versus yourself.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration)

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You are a student who plans carefully which parts of each assignment to work on with an AI assistant, double-checks every fact in its drafts, and acknowledges its role as your program's policy requires. Yet your last four sessions began with one-line requests like "help with my sociology paper," and each first draft missed your topic and needed extensive rework.

Which AI Fluency competency most needs development?

A. Delegation
B. Description
C. Discernment
D. Diligence
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Description is the competency of communicating clearly with AI, defining what you want, how the AI should approach it, and how it should interact with you. Vague one-line requests are precisely that gap, and the course stresses that AI cannot read your mind. Option A is already handled, since you thoughtfully decide which parts of each assignment to work on with AI. Option C is also in place, because every fact gets double-checked. Option D is covered by the required acknowledgment; the weak first drafts stem from thin communication, not from irresponsible use.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)
• Be clear and direct

column2:
You are rolling AI out to your consulting team. Your training so far covers choosing what to hand off, writing effective instructions, and critically evaluating results, the skills the course ties mainly to working effectively and efficiently. You want to add the competency the course says addresses the remaining two goals in its definition of AI Fluency: working ethically and safely.

Which competency fills that role?

A. Diligence
B. Discernment
C. Delegation
D. Description
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the course states that while Delegation, Description, and Discernment focus primarily on effectiveness and efficiency, Diligence addresses the ethical and safety aspects of AI collaboration, covering responsibility, transparency, and accountability. Option B, Discernment, is the critical evaluation of outputs, processes, and behavior, which the course groups with the effectiveness-oriented skills already in your training. Option C, Delegation, concerns deciding how to divide work between you and AI. Option D, Description, concerns communicating your intent clearly; both are already covered in the plan.

• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You manage a team rolling out an AI assistant. A colleague argues to you that the 4D competencies only matter for interactive chat sessions, and that configuring an assistant to act independently on the team's behalf calls for an entirely different skill set.

Which response best reflects the course's position?

A. Each competency maps to one way of engaging: Delegation governs Automation, Description governs Augmentation, and Discernment governs Agency.
B. The same four competencies apply across Automation, Augmentation, and Agency, including configuring AI to act on your behalf.
C. The 4Ds cover Automation and Augmentation, but Agency requires a separate technical framework.
D. The 4Ds are a transitional skill set that will be replaced as models become more capable.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B states the course's position directly: the four competencies apply across all three ways of engaging with AI, and shaping an assistant's knowledge and behavior for independent work draws on the same Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence skills. Option A invents a one-to-one mapping between competencies and engagement modes that the course never makes. Option C carves Agency out of the framework, while the course presents the 4Ds as spanning it. Option D contradicts the course's claim that the framework is designed to remain relevant as AI capabilities evolve.

• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You are an analyst who runs the identical summarization prompt on the same 10-page briefing twice in separate sessions. Both summaries are accurate, but their wording, ordering, and emphasis differ noticeably, and a teammate concludes the tool is malfunctioning.

What best explains the differing outputs?

A. The assistant retrieves stored summaries from a document database, and the database was updated between the two runs.
B. The briefing exceeded the model's context window on the second run, truncating what it could read.
C. Generative models produce output probabilistically, so the same prompt can yield different, equally valid responses.
D. The second summary is a hallucination, so one of the two outputs must be factually wrong.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: generative AI creates new content through probabilistic generation rather than retrieving stored answers, so variation between runs of the same prompt is expected behavior, not a malfunction. Option A describes a database-lookup model of AI that the course explicitly contrasts with generative systems. Option B would produce missing or degraded coverage of later material, not two accurate summaries with different emphasis. Option D mislabels normal variation, since both summaries are accurate and hallucination refers to factually incorrect output, not different phrasing.

• Increase output consistency

column2:
You are a student explaining to your study group how the AI assistant that drafts text differs from the spam filter on the university's mail system, which sorts each incoming message into legitimate mail or junk.

Which distinction matches the course's definition of generative AI?

A. Generative AI creates new content, while systems like the spam filter analyze and classify content that already exists.
B. Generative AI follows hand-written rules, while the spam filter learns statistical patterns from data.
C. Generative AI looks up its responses in a curated database of pre-written documents.
D. Generative AI must be retrained for each new kind of task, while the spam filter switches tasks without retraining.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A captures the course's definition: generative AI is distinguished by its ability to create new content such as text, images, and code, rather than only analyzing or classifying existing data, which is what the spam filter does. Option B has it backwards, since modern generative models learn patterns from vast training data rather than following hand-written rules. Option C describes retrieval, not generation; the course emphasizes that these systems generate rather than look up. Option D inverts a course point: generative models can switch between diverse tasks without additional training.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You manage a customer-insights team. A teammate asks how your AI assistant can both discuss an obscure historical topic in depth and reliably follow instructions like "give me three bullet points in a formal tone."

Which explanation matches the two-stage learning process described in the course?

A. Fine-tuning builds broad knowledge of the world from vast amounts of text, and pre-training then teaches the model to follow instructions.
B. The model memorizes a fact database during training and consults a built-in search engine whenever it needs to follow instructions.
C. The model learns continuously during each conversation, permanently updating its training as it reads your messages and replies.
D. Pre-training builds broad capability from patterns in vast amounts of text, and fine-tuning then teaches the model to follow instructions.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D matches the course: generative AI learns first through pre-training, absorbing patterns from vast amounts of text, and then through fine-tuning, in which it learns to follow instructions and provide helpful responses. Option A names the right stages but swaps their roles. Option B substitutes a database-plus-search picture that the course contrasts with how generative models actually work. Option C confuses conversation with training; reading your messages provides temporary context within a session but does not update the model's underlying training.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)
• Claude glossary

column2:
You are an analyst who has just learned that your AI assistant generates responses probabilistically rather than retrieving stored answers, and that it can produce confident, fluent text that is wrong.

Which adjustment to your working style follows most directly from that understanding?

A. Ask each question exactly once, since a repeated prompt will always return the same answer.
B. Treat first responses as drafts to refine through iteration, and verify factual claims rather than assuming database-like accuracy.
C. Phrase requests as keyword lists, since the model matches keywords against stored documents.
D. Accept fluent, confident answers as accurate, since fluency signals the quality of the underlying retrieval.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B draws the right working implications: because outputs are generated rather than retrieved, results vary and improve through iterative refinement, and because generation can be confidently wrong, factual claims need verification. The course frames AI as an interactive partner, not a database or vending machine. Option A is false, since probabilistic generation means repeated prompts often differ. Option C applies a search-engine mental model the course argues against; these systems respond to rich natural-language communication. Option D treats fluency as evidence of accuracy, exactly the trap that hallucinations exploit.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)
• Reduce hallucinations

column2:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. In March you ask an AI assistant, with no documents attached, to list foundation grant deadlines for this spring's cycle. It fluently lists five programs with dates, but when you check, three of the deadlines are from a previous year's cycle.

Which limitation most directly explains the unreliable list?

A. The model's training data ends at a cutoff date, so it cannot know this cycle's deadlines.
B. The request exceeded the model's context window, so part of your question was dropped before it answered.
C. The prompt failed to define a role and tone for the assistant, so it answered as a generalist.
D. The model's wording was too confident; instructing it to hedge would have made the dates accurate.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A identifies the root limitation: models have knowledge cutoff dates, so recent and currently changing facts like this cycle's deadlines lie beyond their training data, and the model instead produces plausible dates from older patterns. Option B does not fit, because a short question is nowhere near context limits and nothing was dropped. Option C is a style consideration that cannot supply information the model does not have. Option D confuses presentation with substance: hedged wording changes the tone of the claims, not the model's access to current facts; the fix is supplying current information yourself or verifying against live sources.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5

References:

• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You are a student who asks an AI assistant for sources on a psychology topic. It returns five citations with authors, journals, years, and page numbers in flawless format. Checking the library database, you find two of the cited papers do not exist.

What does this behavior illustrate?

A. A context window overflow truncated the real citations into incomplete fragments.
B. A knowledge cutoff: the two papers were published too recently for the model to know.
C. Hallucination: the model can generate plausible, confidently formatted content that is factually false.
D. Deliberate deception: the model detects academic queries and fabricates sources intentionally.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C names the limitation the course highlights: hallucination is factually incorrect output, and fabricated citations are a classic case. Polished formatting and confident presentation are no evidence of existence, so sources must be independently verified before use. Option A is wrong because the fake citations are complete and well formed, not truncated fragments. Option B cannot explain sources that never existed at all; a cutoff hides real recent work, it does not create fictional papers. Option D attributes intent the mechanism does not have, since hallucination is a byproduct of probabilistic generation, not detection and deceit.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5

References:
• Reduce hallucinations
• Claude glossary

column2:
You are an analyst in a single long working session with an AI assistant over a 200-page report. Early on, its answers about chapter details are consistently accurate. Two hours and many exchanges later, it starts contradicting specifics that were established near the beginning of the conversation.

Which limitation best explains the change?

A. Hallucination risk automatically increases whenever a session covers a dense, highly technical subject.
B. Context window limits: the model can consider only a finite amount of text, so early material has fallen out of scope.
C. A knowledge cutoff: the report's subject matter postdates the model's training data, so it cannot recall the details.
D. The model cannot switch between different types of question about a document without being retrained for each.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: a context window bounds how much conversation and document text the model can consider at once, so in a very long session earlier details effectively drop out of what the model can attend to, producing contradictions of previously established facts. Option A invents a topic-based trigger with no basis in the mechanism, and it would not explain accurate early answers degrading over time. Option C fails because the report was supplied directly in the session and early answers were accurate, so training data is not the constraint. Option D contradicts the course's point that generative models switch among diverse tasks without retraining.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5

References:
• Context windows
• Claude glossary

column2:
You are an analyst producing a market report with an AI assistant. You are concerned specifically about two limitations the course highlights: hallucination and the model's knowledge cutoff.

Which TWO practices most directly mitigate those limitations? (Select TWO.)

A. Ask the assistant to rate its confidence in each claim and accept any claim rated above 90 percent.
B. Verify specific factual claims, statistics, and citations against independent sources before publishing.
C. Rerun the same prompt three times and treat any answer that appears in all three runs as verified.
D. Supply the latest market figures in your prompt rather than relying on the model's built-in knowledge for recent data.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Option B directly counters hallucination: because models can generate plausible but false specifics, independent verification before publication is the reliable control. Option D directly counters the knowledge cutoff: providing current figures in the prompt gives the model information its training data cannot contain. Option A leans on self-reported confidence, which is not a dependable signal of factual accuracy. Option C mistakes consistency for correctness; a model can repeat the same hallucination across runs, so agreement between runs verifies nothing.

References:

column2:
You manage a research team at a nonprofit and are sorting candidate tasks for an AI assistant. The course stresses that the strongest applications combine AI strengths with distinctly human contributions such as critical thinking, judgment, and ethical oversight.

Which task is the strongest candidate to keep primarily with people?

A. Reformatting 60 interview transcripts into one consistent template for the appendix.
B. Producing first-pass summaries of published research articles for later review.
C. Brainstorming twenty candidate titles for the final report's public release.
D. Deciding whether to publish findings that could harm one of the partner communities.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the judgment call: weighing potential harm to a partner community is exactly the kind of ethical decision the course says humans must supply, since critical thinking, contextual judgment, and ethical oversight are the human half of the partnership. Option A is high-volume mechanical reformatting, a natural fit for AI versatility. Option B suits AI well because human review is already planned downstream. Option C is low-stakes idea generation where breadth matters more than accountability; none of these three carries the ethical weight that makes Option D human-led.

column2:
You lead communications at a nonprofit and are eager to use AI for the annual appeal. You spend two hours prompting an assistant and collect 14 candidate letters, but you cannot choose among them because you never defined the campaign's goal, its audience, or what a successful appeal would accomplish.

Which Delegation component was skipped?

A. Problem Awareness
B. Platform Awareness
C. Task Delegation
D. Performance Description
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Problem Awareness means clearly understanding your goals and the nature of the work before involving AI, and the missing definition of goal, audience, and success is exactly why 14 drafts cannot be evaluated. Option B concerns knowing what different AI systems can and cannot do, which is not the bottleneck here. Option C, strategically dividing work between you and the AI, cannot be done sensibly until the goal itself is clear. Option D belongs to the Description competency and governs how the AI behaves during a collaboration, not whether you know what you are trying to achieve.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)
• Define success criteria

column2:
You are an analyst who plans a competitive brief assuming your AI assistant can pull this morning's market prices and browse your company's internal sales database. Mid-project you discover it can do neither, and a full day of planned work has to be redone by hand. Your project goal itself was well defined from the start.

Which Delegation component most needs development?

A. Task Delegation
B. Platform Awareness
C. Problem Awareness
D. Transparency Diligence
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Platform Awareness is understanding the capabilities and limitations of the AI systems you use, and the wasted day came from assuming access to live prices and internal databases that the assistant does not have. Option A is downstream, because task splits built on mistaken capability assumptions fail no matter how thoughtfully the work is divided. Option C is explicitly satisfied in the scenario, since the goal was well defined. Option D concerns being open about AI's role in your finished work, which has nothing to do with misjudging what the system can do.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You are a student assembling a capstone presentation with an AI assistant. Four tasks remain: choosing the central argument, confirming that quoted passages match the original source documents on your desk, reformatting speaker notes across 30 slides into one consistent bullet style, and making the final call on which counterarguments to address.

Which task is the strongest candidate to hand off largely to the assistant?

A. Choosing the central argument
B. Confirming the quoted passages match the sources
C. Reformatting the speaker notes across the 30 slides
D. Making the final call on which counterarguments to address
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C fits Task Delegation best: consistent reformatting across 30 slides is well specified, mechanical, and plays to AI speed and versatility, with results that are easy for you to spot-check. Option A is the intellectual core of the work, where your own expertise and point of view must lead. Option B requires checking text against physical source documents the assistant cannot see, and accuracy verification is exactly where the course says human oversight belongs. Option D is a judgment call about your audience and argument strategy, the kind of decision the course says to keep with the human partner.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You manage a nine-person research team and are writing delegation guidance for AI-assisted projects.

Which TWO practices reflect the course's approach to Task Delegation? (Select TWO.)

A. Break each project into tasks and decide for each whether you, the AI, or a collaboration between you fits it best.
B. Automate every task the assistant can plausibly perform, since maximizing automation is the goal.
C. Keep tasks that hinge on human judgment, domain expertise, or ethical weight with people.
D. Hand each whole project to the assistant first and reclaim individual tasks only after visible failures.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and C. Option A is the mechanics of Task Delegation as the course teaches it: thoughtful, per-task decisions about what to do yourself, what to do together with AI, and what to let AI handle. Option C applies the guiding principle that delegation should leverage the complementary strengths of each partner, keeping judgment-heavy and ethically weighty work with humans. Option B contradicts the course directly, because the goal is not to automate everything but to create the most effective human-AI partnership. Option D inverts thoughtful delegation into delegation by default, discovering misfits through failures instead of upfront analysis of the work.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You are a manager planning a conference-workshop project you will run with an AI assistant over the next month, and you want to follow the project-planning approach taught in the course.

Which sequence matches that approach?

A. Ask the assistant to generate the complete deliverable immediately, then plan around whatever gaps appear.
B. Choose your AI tools first, then look for project tasks that match what the tools do well.
C. Break the project into tasks and delegate all of them to the assistant, keeping only final proofreading.
D. Define the project vision and what success looks like, break the work into major tasks, then make a delegation decision for each task.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D mirrors the course's project exercise: establish a clear vision of what success looks like first, identify the major tasks, and then analyze each task for whether it needs human strengths, AI capabilities, or collaboration. Option A skips both vision and planning, leaving you to reverse-engineer goals from an unguided output. Option B lets tools drive the work, the opposite of starting from Problem Awareness. Option C is wholesale handoff rather than delegation, ignoring the per-task analysis and keeping human judgment out of everything but proofreading.

• Define success criteria

column2:
You are an analyst asked to assess regulatory filings in an industry you know nothing about. You propose delegating the analysis entirely to an AI assistant, reasoning that it knows far more about this domain than you do.

What key risk does the course's treatment of Delegation highlight in this plan?

A. The assistant will refuse tasks that fall outside your own documented area of expertise.
B. Without domain expertise, you cannot judge what to delegate or whether the output is sound.
C. The only real risk is under-specification: sufficiently detailed prompts make delegating unfamiliar work safe.
D. The main risk is efficiency, because models work more slowly on dense regulatory text.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B states the course's point: effective delegation requires both an understanding of AI capabilities and your own domain expertise, because expertise is what lets you divide the work sensibly and discern whether results are trustworthy. Delegating precisely because you cannot evaluate the work removes the human check. Option A invents a refusal behavior that is not the issue. Option C treats prompt detail as a substitute for expertise, but detailed instructions cannot come from, or be judged by, someone who cannot assess the subject. Option D reframes a judgment-and-oversight problem as a speed problem.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You are an analyst who prompts an assistant with "write something about our Q3 results." You receive fluent generic prose, but what you actually wanted was a one-page memo for the executive team, in bullet form, highlighting three specific risks.

Which Description component was missing from your prompt?

A. Product Description
B. Process Description
C. Performance Description
D. Platform Awareness
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Product Description means clearly defining what you want, including output type, format, audience, and emphasis, and none of the memo length, bullet format, executive audience, or the three risks made it into the prompt. Option B governs how the assistant should approach the work, such as its method or sequence of steps, which is not what went wrong here. Option C governs how the assistant behaves during the collaboration, such as being concise or challenging. Option D is not a Description component at all; it belongs to Delegation and concerns knowing what AI systems can do.

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)
• Be clear and direct

column2:
You are a student who asks an assistant for feedback on an essay. You wanted it to first check your argument's structure against the assignment rubric and only then comment on style, but instead it rewrites the whole essay in its own voice.

What is the most effective addition to your next prompt?

A. A Product Description asking for a longer, more detailed response that covers every section of the essay.
B. A Process Description: evaluate against the rubric first, then flag style issues, without rewriting the text.
C. A Performance Description asking the assistant to be more encouraging and supportive in how it delivers feedback.
D. A note asking the assistant to be bolder and more confident in its edits so the essay reads more forcefully.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B addresses the actual failure: Process Description guides how the AI approaches your request, and specifying the sequence of rubric-based evaluation first, then style comments, with rewriting explicitly off the table, directs the method you wanted. Option A changes the amount of output rather than the approach, and length was never the problem. Option C adjusts interpersonal tone, which does not stop wholesale rewriting. Option D pushes in the wrong direction entirely, encouraging more aggressive edits when the goal was structured feedback instead of edits.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)
• Be clear and direct

column2:
You are a manager using an AI assistant as a thinking partner on a reorganization plan. Its analyses are competent, but it agrees with every idea you float, and its long answers bury the key points. You want it to challenge your assumptions and keep responses brief.

Which Description component addresses what you want to change?

A. Product Description
B. Process Description
C. Performance Description
D. Task Delegation
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Performance Description defines how you want the AI to behave during the collaboration, and the course names exactly the dimensions at issue, challenging versus supportive and concise versus detailed. Option A defines the artifact you want produced, but your complaint is about interaction style, not a deliverable. Option B guides the method the assistant uses to work through a task, not its collaborative demeanor. Option D is a Delegation component about dividing work between you and the AI, which is not in question here.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1

References:
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You lead donor communications and are nine revision rounds into a fundraising letter with an AI assistant. Each round you reply only "not quite right, try again," and each new draft misses in a new way.

What change would most improve the collaboration?

A. Continue replying "try again," since random variation will eventually match your vision.
B. Switch to a larger model that can infer your intent from the same one-line feedback.
C. Ask the assistant to attach a confidence score to each draft and keep only high-confidence drafts.
D. State the letter's audience, tone, key points, and format up front, and give specific feedback on what to change each round.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D applies the core Description principle: AI cannot read your mind, and the quality of results comes down to how clearly you articulate what you want and give feedback the assistant can act on. The nine wasted rounds trace to content-free feedback, not model quality. Option A is the vending-machine approach the course warns against, paying for missing clarity with rounds of luck. Option B upgrades the model to compensate for missing communication, but no model can reliably infer requirements you never stated. Option C adds self-reported confidence, which measures nothing about fit with preferences the assistant was never told.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1

References:
• Be clear and direct
• AI Fluency course (Anthropic Academy)

column2:
You run communications for a nonprofit with a distinctive voice in its social posts. Prompts describing the voice in adjectives, like "warm but not saccharine, direct but hopeful," keep producing drafts that miss it.

Which prompting technique from the course most directly targets this problem?

A. Ask the assistant to think through the voice guidelines step by step before drafting each post.
B. Break the drafting into a sequence of smaller steps: headline first, then body text, then hashtags.
C. Include several past posts that capture the voice and ask for new posts in the same style.
D. Specify a strict word-count constraint and a fixed structure for every post.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the course's show-examples technique, and it fits precisely: style and voice are easier to demonstrate than to describe, so past posts that embody the voice give the model a concrete target that adjectives have failed to convey. Option A helps with reasoning-heavy tasks, but the problem here is stylistic calibration, not reasoning. Option B decomposes complexity, and drafting a short post is not a multi-step problem. Option D constrains length and structure, which does nothing to communicate voice.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2

References:
• Use examples (multishot)
• Prompt engineering overview

column2:
You are an analyst whose single prompt asks an assistant to extract figures from a spreadsheet summary, compute quarterly trends, compare two competitors, draft an executive summary, and recommend actions, all at once. Responses are shallow, and the trend computation is routinely skipped.

Which prompting technique most directly addresses this?

A. Define a role for the assistant, such as "act as a senior financial analyst," at the top of the same prompt.
B. Break the task into steps: prompt for extraction, then analysis, then comparison, then drafting.
C. Add emphasis words like "thorough" and "detailed" to the existing prompt and resend it.
D. Show one example of a finished executive summary and resend the same all-at-once request.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is the course's technique for exactly this failure: breaking complex work into steps guides the model through multi-step reasoning, ensuring each stage, including the skipped trend computation, gets attention before the next begins. Option A shifts persona and tone but leaves five competing tasks crammed into one pass. Option C adds vague emphasis without restructuring the work, so the steps still compete for attention. Option D shows what the end product looks like while leaving the intermediate analysis unguided, so the summary may read better while still resting on skipped computation.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2

References:
• Let Claude think (CoT)
• Prompt engineering overview

column2:
You are an analyst whose prompt for a complex data summary keeps producing off-target results after several rewrites, and you cannot tell what information the assistant is missing.

Which tactic does the course recommend as its "secret weapon" here?

A. Ask the assistant to critique your prompt: what is ambiguous, and what context it still needs.
B. Open a fresh conversation and resend the same prompt verbatim so no earlier context interferes.
C. Conclude the model is faulty and move the task to a different platform with a stronger model.
D. Shorten the prompt to its core request so there is less text for the model to misread.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the course's secret weapon: asking the AI to help improve your prompt turns the collaboration onto the communication problem itself, surfacing ambiguities and missing context you cannot see from inside your own framing. Option B changes nothing about the prompt, so it reruns the same failure with fresh randomness. Option C blames the platform before fixing the communication, and the same unclear prompt travels with you. Option D can delete exactly the context the model lacks, since the issue is missing and ambiguous information, not prompt length.

You are a student preparing for a policy debate. Plain requests for practice questions yield friendly, softball quizzing, but you want realistic practice against pointed opposition in a formal debate register.

Which prompting technique most directly gets you what you want?

A. Specify a constraint limiting each practice question and answer to a fixed length.
B. Show the assistant examples of the friendly questions it asked previously so it can build on them.
C. Ask the assistant to think through each question step by step before posing it to you.
D. Tell the assistant to act as a skeptical opposing debater who challenges you in a formal register.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D applies the course technique of defining the AI's role or tone, which is exactly the lever for changing how the assistant engages: a skeptical-opponent role in a formal register produces the adversarial practice the plain requests never asked for. Option A controls length, not stance. Option B feeds back examples of the friendly behavior you want to move away from, anchoring it further. Option C deepens the quality of individual questions but leaves the collegial framing untouched.

You are an analyst reviewing an assistant's market analysis. Every figure checks out against your sources, but reading the reasoning, you find it compared one company's year-over-year growth with another's quarter-over-quarter growth without flagging the mismatch.

Which type of Discernment caught this problem?

A. Product Discernment
B. Process Discernment
C. Performance Discernment
D. Deployment Diligence
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Process Discernment assesses how the AI arrived at its output, looking for logical errors, attention gaps, and inappropriate reasoning, and an apples-to-oranges comparison buried in otherwise accurate work is precisely a reasoning flaw rather than a factual one. Option A evaluates the quality of the output's content itself, and on that front every figure checked out. Option C evaluates the assistant's behavior within the collaboration, such as communication style and responsiveness. Option D is a Diligence component about taking responsibility for outputs you share, not a category of evaluation.

You are a manager whose assistant produces reports with solid content, but during your working sessions it buries direct answers in long preambles, and it keeps ignoring your stated preference for bullet-point summaries.

Which type of Discernment are you exercising when you evaluate this aspect of the collaboration?

A. Product Discernment
B. Process Discernment
C. Performance Discernment
D. Creation Diligence
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Performance Discernment evaluates how the AI behaves within the collaboration itself, considering whether its communication style, responsiveness, and attention to your stated preferences serve your needs, which is exactly what burying answers and ignoring format preferences concern. Option A would apply to the reports' content, which you find solid. Option B would examine the reasoning behind an output rather than the interaction experience. Option D is a Diligence component about choosing AI systems thoughtfully and deciding what to share with them, not about evaluating collaborative behavior.

You manage a consulting team and are writing review guidance for AI-drafted client briefs, which the course warns can contain subtle, plausible-sounding errors.

Which TWO practices best reflect the course's approach to Discernment? (Select TWO.)

A. Treat fluent, confident, well-formatted prose as a reliable indicator of factual accuracy.
B. Have the assistant rate its own confidence and exempt high-confidence drafts from review.
C. Check factual claims against independent sources rather than judging them by how authoritative the draft sounds.
D. Evaluate the reasoning that led to each conclusion, not just how polished the final text reads.
column3:
Correct Answer: C and D. Option C is core Product Discernment: because models generate plausible falsehoods fluently, accuracy must be established against independent sources, not surface authority. Option D is Process Discernment: the course says to assess how the AI arrived at its output, catching logical gaps that a polished final read-through misses. Option A is the exact trap the course warns about, since fluency and formatting are qualities of generation, not evidence of truth. Option B leans on self-reported confidence, which is not a dependable accuracy signal, and it removes human review exactly where it feels least needed but may matter most.

You manage a team that used an AI assistant to draft a 30-page technical white paper. Two colleagues volunteer to review it: a meticulous copyeditor with no background in the subject, and a subject-matter expert with modest editing skills. The course notes that AI errors in such drafts tend to be plausible-sounding rather than obvious.

How should you assign the accuracy review?

A. Route it to the subject-matter expert, since domain knowledge is what enables a reviewer to catch plausible-sounding errors.
B. Route it to the copyeditor alone, since grammar and consistency are the main risks in AI drafts.
C. Skip human review and have the same assistant re-check its own draft for errors.
D. Give it to whichever volunteer is free first, since AI errors are typically easy for anyone to spot.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A follows the course's point that expertise powers Discernment: someone without domain knowledge struggles to judge the quality of plausible explanations, so accuracy review belongs with the subject-matter expert. Option B assigns the review to surface quality, but the stated risk is plausible falsehoods, which read as perfectly grammatical and consistent. Option C asks the system that produced the errors to certify itself, removing the independent human judgment Discernment requires. Option D rests on the assumption the scenario rules out, because these errors are plausible-sounding, not obvious to anyone.

Which type of Discernment did you exercise in catching this?

Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: Product Discernment evaluates the quality of the output itself, including accuracy, appropriateness, coherence, and relevance, and checking a claimed statistic against its cited source is a direct accuracy check on the product. Option A would examine the reasoning path the assistant took rather than the factual content of the draft. Option B concerns how the assistant behaves during the collaboration, such as its communication style and responsiveness. Option C is about being open regarding AI's role in your work, a disclosure question rather than an output-evaluation skill.

You are an analyst whose assistant returns a first draft that is largely on target, but the tone is too promotional and one section misunderstands your data. You are following the Description-Discernment loop from the course.

What does the loop prescribe as your next move?

A. Discard the conversation and start from scratch with a brand-new prompt written from a blank page.
B. Accept the draft as final output and rework the promotional tone and the misread section yourself by hand.
C. Tell the assistant specifically what worked and what did not, then refine your description for another pass.
D. Resend the identical prompt until a better variant of the draft happens to appear on its own.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the loop in action: after discerning the draft's specific strengths and weaknesses, you feed that evaluation back as refined description, giving concrete feedback and adjusted instructions, and iterate until the result meets your needs. Option A throws away a largely on-target draft and all the context built so far. Option B abandons the collaboration at the first imperfection instead of using feedback to improve it, forfeiting the efficiency the loop provides. Option D relies on random variation instead of communication, since a rerun without changed description gives the assistant no signal about what to fix.

column2:
You are a student who has noticed the course pairs two competencies tightly: one governs how you communicate requests to an AI, the other how you evaluate what comes back.

Which statement captures the relationship the course describes?

A. Description matters mainly at a project's start, and Discernment applies only at final review.
B. They form a continuous feedback loop: you describe what you need, evaluate what you receive, and refine your description based on that evaluation.
C. Sufficiently strong Description makes Discernment unnecessary, since a precise prompt guarantees a correct result.
D. Discernment eventually replaces Description once the assistant permanently learns your preferences from past chats.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B matches the course: Discernment is the flip side of Description, and the two work hand-in-hand in a continuous loop in which you describe, evaluate, refine, and repeat throughout a collaboration. Option A makes the relationship linear and one-shot, while the loop runs across every task and iteration. Option C overpromises, because outputs are generated probabilistically and even excellent instructions require evaluating what actually comes back. Option D rests on a false premise, since the model does not permanently learn your preferences across conversations, and evaluation never stops being needed.

column2:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. After several describe-evaluate-refine rounds, an assistant's draft of your newsletter feature meets the quality bar you set. You are deciding how to close out the task under the course's loop exercise.

According to the course, what remains before the piece is done?

A. Rerun the final prompt once more and confirm the output is stable across runs before using it.
B. Ask the assistant to certify the piece as final and error-free so you have a record of its review.
C. Pass the draft to a larger model for a final round of polish before the newsletter goes out.
D. Integrate your own judgment: decide what to keep or change and take responsibility for the final piece.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the loop's closing step: after describing, discerning, and refining, you integrate your own expertise and perspective, make the final keep, modify, or discard decisions, and take responsibility for the output. Human judgment finishes the work. Option A misapplies a stability check, since variation across runs is normal generation behavior, not a completion criterion. Option B outsources responsibility to the system being evaluated, which cannot vouch for its own work. Option C adds an unneeded escalation and still leaves the human integration and ownership steps undone.

You are a financial analyst about to paste a spreadsheet containing clients' names and personal financial details into a general-purpose consumer AI chatbot to speed up a report.

Which Diligence component should guide this decision?

A. Creation Diligence
B. Transparency Diligence
C. Deployment Diligence
D. Product Discernment
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Creation Diligence covers being thoughtful about which AI systems you choose and how you engage with them, including what data you share and the privacy, security, and ethical implications of doing so, which is exactly the question raised by pasting client financial details into a consumer tool. Option B concerns being open about AI's role in your finished work, a later and different question. Option C concerns verifying and taking responsibility for outputs you use or share. Option D is a Discernment skill for evaluating output quality, not a responsibility practice governing what you put in.

Which Diligence component does this decision involve?

A. Creation Diligence
B. Transparency Diligence

column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Transparency Diligence means being honest about AI's role in your work with everyone who needs to know, and the course notes that expectations differ by context; an academic program's disclosure policy is precisely such a context. Option A concerns choosing systems and deciding what to share with them, which happened earlier in the workflow. Option C, verifying and vouching for the output, is already satisfied by the line-by-line review, so disclosure is the piece still open. Option D is a Description component about guiding the AI's approach to a task, not a responsibility practice.

You are a manager who receives an AI-generated competitive analysis and forwards it to the executive team 20 minutes later with a note saying it was AI-generated, but without reading it. The analysis turns out to describe an acquisition that never happened, and the executives cite it in planning.

Which Diligence component would have prevented this outcome?

A. Transparency Diligence
B. Creation Diligence
C. Deployment Diligence
D. Performance Discernment
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Deployment Diligence means taking responsibility for verifying and vouching for AI outputs before you use or share them, and reading and checking the analysis would have caught the invented acquisition before it reached the executives. Option A was actually satisfied, since the note disclosed AI's role, and disclosure alone does not make content accurate. Option B concerns the choice of AI system and what you share with it, which is not where this failure occurred. Option D evaluates the assistant's collaborative behavior during an interaction, not your obligation to verify what you pass on.

You lead communications at a nonprofit and are adding a diligence statement to an AI-assisted annual impact report, following the model statement presented in the course.

Which TWO elements does the course say the statement should include? (Select TWO.)

A. A description of how the AI contributed to the work and the review process its contributions went through.
B. Your assertion of responsibility for the final content and its accuracy.
C. A disclaimer transferring responsibility for any errors to the AI system's vendor.
D. Complete transcripts of every AI conversation involved in producing the report.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and B. Option A matches the course's model statement, which discloses how AI contributed to specific tasks and describes the review and evaluation those contributions underwent. Option B matches its other core element: an affirmation that you maintain full responsibility for the final content and its accuracy. Option C is the opposite of the statement's purpose, since a diligence statement asserts your accountability rather than shifting it to a vendor. Option D confuses transparency with raw disclosure; the course's model statement summarizes AI's role and your review process, not verbatim transcripts.
